analysis.one_liner: Bans airlines from paying workers bonuses for charging passengers add-on fees and from charging fees that discriminate by disability or family status.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee with no cosponsors and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban airlines from paying employees, contractors, or agents any incentive tied directly to getting passengers to pay extra fees for bags, seats, or other add-ons. It would also prohibit airlines from charging passengers different fares or fees based on disability status, family status, or characteristics already protected in airline law. It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers. The bill would make it illegal for airlines to pay employees or contractors bonuses for extracting baggage, seat-selection, and similar add-on fees from travelers, so pricing pressure at the counter and gate would ease. It would also bar airlines from charging passengers with disabilities or traveling with children differently for the same service on the same flight.

how_it_helps.text: Bans airlines from paying any employee, contractor, or agent an incentive given as a direct result of requiring a passenger to pay an add-on fee for baggage, seating, or similar services [S2].

Prohibits airlines from discriminating on the basis of disability status, familial status, or other covered characteristics when charging or setting fares or ancillary fees for the same service on the same flight [S2].
Covers a broad list of add-on services, including seating, baggage, food, early boarding, lounge access, and wifi [S2].
Includes a rule of construction making clear airlines may still allow children to fly free or at a discount, so the anti-discrimination rule does not eliminate family discounts [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and foreign carriers flying to the U.S. bear the cost: they could no longer pay staff commissions or bonuses for selling baggage, seating, and other add-on fees, and could no longer charge different fees based on disability, family status, or other covered characteristics. Their ancillary fee revenue would shrink.

drawbacks.text: The bill was a one-senator proposal with no cosponsors [S3] and no committee action [S4], so it never received scrutiny or refinement on points like how a ban on incentives would be enforced or how it would distinguish fee-based incentives from ordinary sales commissions.

Banning incentives tied directly to add-on fee sales could push airlines to raise base fares to recover the revenue, leaving passengers paying roughly the same total through a different structure rather than seeing costs fall [S2].

The anti-discrimination clause could invite litigation over whether a fee difference is a prohibited discrimination or a legitimate discount, such as child fares, though the bill carves out free or reduced children's fares explicitly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is straightforward and targets a real, widely felt cost: add-on fees pushed on travelers by staff whose pay depends on selling them, plus fee differences for disabled passengers and families. The main cost falls on airline ancillary fee revenue, and the largest honest caveat is that airlines could shift revenue into base fares, so passengers' total ticket costs might not fall much even if the fee practices end. The bill is narrow rather than a broad junk-fee overhaul, which limits both its benefit and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and no one ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Hawley introduced the bill on December 10, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day [S1] [S4].

The bill text would prohibit air carriers from paying any employee, contractor, or agent a benefit given as a direct result of requiring a passenger to pay an add-on fee for baggage, seating, or similar services, and would bar fee discrimination based on disability status, familial status, or other covered characteristics [S2].
No cosponsor ever signed on [S3], and the complete action history shows no committee hearing, markup, or floor action [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee or the Senate voting on the bill [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines, which keep collecting tens of billions of dollars in baggage, seat-selection, and other add-on fees and can continue paying staff and contractors incentives for selling them. Passengers who would have benefited from the ban are no better off.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 5470, the End Airline Extortion Act, to ban airline employee incentives for add-on fees and fee discrimination against disabled passengers and families

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no recorded action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no committee action or votes followed.

industries.note: Baggage, seat-selection, and other ancillary fees are a major airline revenue stream, and incentive pay tied to selling those fees is central to how carriers push them. The bill would cut into that revenue, so the industry's interest in killing the bill ran against passengers' interest in lower add-on costs.

industries.industry: Foreign air carriers serving U.S. routes
industries.note: The prohibition applies equally to foreign air carriers operating U.S. flights, so foreign carriers selling seat and bag add-ons would face the same limits.
